name: Iris Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fast. I'm doing computer science with a data track, and I live at home with my dad and my grandfather in a small town about forty minutes from campus by train, so I do a lot of coding on the train. Four days of classes, then three evenings a week I work in the kitchen at a pizza place, which is loud and hot and weirdly relaxing. I've got a notes app with a list of things I want to try, and I tick one off most weeks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's on that list at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Training a tiny model to guess pizza orders for the restaurant, mostly as a joke, and getting a reading group going for first-years. I use an AI assistant for nearly everything, from debugging to planning my week. It saves me an hour a day, and I use that hour to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it's a useful tool and I'd carry on using it. I'd tell people that the hype's loud, but the daily reality is smaller, like a better autocomplete. At the pizza place it's already sorting our orders by prep time and the chef just says 'fine, whatever works'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pretty relaxed about the technology, but I'd still have the usual things in my head. My dad works nights at a depot, and he's hurt his back twice. My loan and the train fare eat most of what I earn, so I'm never ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, probably build more side projects, and apply for a summer internship in data. I'd keep an eye on the train fare and try for a student rail pass. And I'd put a bit of every pay packet aside, since the depot's hours aren't safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content, but not totally easy. A normal world means my skills still count and my family still has the same worries as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the family worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad's back, mainly. If my dad's back goes, the depot won't keep his job open, and it won't matter whether AI is hype or not. I'd be the one expected to help, and I'm on a student loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you help him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take more shifts at the pizza place, and look into whether the university has a hardship fund for family emergencies. I'd also learn his insurance paperwork so he isn't doing it alone.

say: I'd say it's a useful **tool** and I'd carry on using it.
I'd say the daily reality is smaller than the **hype**, more like better autocomplete.
think: I'm relaxed about the technology, but my **dad's back** and the loan weigh on me.
The loan and train fare eat most of my pay, so I'm never **ahead**.
do: Build more **side projects** and apply for a summer data internship.
Look for a student **rail pass** to cut train costs.
Put a bit of each **pay packet** aside.
feel: **Content** but not easy, since my family's worries don't go away.
S0.quote: If my dad's back goes, the depot won't keep his job open, and it won't matter whether AI is hype or not
fieldNote: The worry is her **dad's** job and back, not AI.
She treats AI as a **daily tool** that saves an hour, which she reinvests in projects.
Her **money** is stretched by train fares and the loan.

steps.text: Apply for a summer data internship
Ask for a student rail pass to cut train costs
Set aside ten percent of every pizza shift pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be messy but manageable, and that the people who learn to use the tools well will be fine. I'd tell my reading group that it's changing what a junior does, so we should think about the parts only a person can do. I'd also say we shouldn't just accept 'it's inevitable', and that companies and governments need to tell people what's happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in the right place, but not guaranteed. The card says coding and checking are first in line, and the exact entry-level job I'd apply for is the thing that shrinks. I'd need to be the person who understands the data and the people, not just the code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go deeper into data and statistics rather than only coding, and I'd take on a small project for a real client, even for free. I'd run my reading group more seriously so I'd know people who are hiring. And I'd keep tutoring myself on new tools every month so I'm not left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit tense. It's like being at the start of a race where nobody knows the route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by understanding the people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knowing why a restaurant owner wants an answer and what they'd do with it. A model that guesses pizza orders is cheap, but knowing why the chef changes the menu on Fridays is what makes it useful. I want to be good at that part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the pizza place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owner, Luca, would probably use AI for ordering and scheduling first. He'd cut a couple of part-time shifts, and mine could be one. I'd have to keep a second source of money, like tutoring.

say: I'd say it's messy but **manageable**, and the people who learn the tools will be fine.
I'd tell my reading group to focus on what only a **person** can do.

steps.text: Take a statistics module and a data project next term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, honestly, that nobody's ready, including me. Two years is less than my degree. I'd tell people to calm down but also not to ignore it, and then I'd feel like I was lying a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the plan I had, a degree and then a junior data job, stops existing. By the time I graduate, my entry-level role is something a model does faster. I'd be paying a loan for a ticket that's already been cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start two things at once. First, build a real product that makes money or at least shows what I can do, because ownership might matter more than employment. Second, look at what the hands-on world needs in that window, like installing and maintaining automated systems, because robots come about three years later and someone has to set them up. And I'd tell my dad we need to talk about money, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Adrenaline mostly. I'd also feel sick if I thought about my dad's back and the loan. I'd probably sleep badly for a couple of weeks and then get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the honest talk with your dad sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Short and awkward. I'd tell my dad that nobody in our family has been through this before, so we should check every bill together on Sunday night. He'd tease me, then show me the spreadsheet he's been hiding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would a product matter more than a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if the thinking work is cheap, the scarce thing is knowing what to build and who wants it. A small product shows I can do that. A CV doesn't.

I'd tell people to calm down but not **ignore** it.

steps.text: Build and launch a small paid order-forecast tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to react but only if people actually start. I'd tell my friends to get their hands dirty with the tools now and build things, not wait for permission. I'd also say that we should ask who benefits from the change, and push for something fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel okay. I'd have most of a degree by the time it lands, and I'd have built things before it does. The loan is still a drag, but five years gives me room to get ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the degree and add a placement, probably at a small firm so I get real responsibilities. I'd use AI to move faster on my own projects and ship at least two real ones before I graduate. I'd also set up a savings goal for my dad's back surgery fund, because the worry about it won't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Upbeat but alert. There's a timer on it, and I like the idea of using the time well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a small firm for the placement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in a small firm you do five jobs and see how the whole thing runs. A big company gives you one small box to work in, but a small firm lets you see why the customers pay. That's the part that survives change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change if it was two years instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the placement and go for money and independence. Five years lets me learn, and two years means I'd need to earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth and last picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and the interesting question is what we build in that time. I'd tell my friends that the transition could be decent if we shape it. Online I'd probably share what I'm working on and ask for ideas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be calm about myself. By 28 I could have a job I like, a bit of savings, and a few projects behind me. I'd worry for my grandfather, who'd be in his late eighties, and for dad, who'd be near retirement but with a bad back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and take a placement. I'd learn the tools as they change and start a small business on the side with friends from my reading group. I'd also put money aside for my dad's retirement help, because the pension there isn't great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. I'd also be a bit impatient, because ten years sounds like a lot, and I'm someone who likes things now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you keep yourself from coasting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yearly check-ins with a friend, where we say what we did. My reading group would be my accountability, because it's hard to bluff to people who've seen your last three projects. We'd do it over pizza.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for your dad specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay for a physio course early, so his back doesn't force him out. If I have the money by then, it's the best thing I could do.

I'd tell friends the transition could be **decent** if we shape it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it takes away my time to build a track record before the ground moves. What would help is quick access to retraining and a way to keep paying rent while I switch, and real information from companies about what they plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think using AI daily means I don't worry. I use AI every day, but I still check every number it gives me, because I'm the one who answers for the mistakes. That's a habit worth keeping.

headlineQuote: I use AI every day, but I still check every number it gives me, because I'm the one who answers for the mistakes
portrait: Iris is an **18-year-old** computer science first-year who lives with her dad and grandfather and works in a pizza kitchen.
She is centrist and adaptive: she uses AI tools every day and builds side projects every week.
Her main worry is her **dad's** back and the family's thin money, not the technology itself.
She plans by building products, joining small firms and putting aside part of every pay packet.
Her mood is mostly uneasy, rising to anxious at two years and falling to calm with ten.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries her most, because it removes the time to build a track record.
whatWouldHelp: She wants fast **retraining**, rent support while switching, and honest information from firms.
